script_data.title: How Moon Landings Were Woven by Hand
script_data.description: Discover how NASA relied on textile workers to hand-weave the computer code that landed Apollo 11 on the Moon. Would you trust hand-woven software for space travel? 🚀💻
script_data.script:
Mind-bending Paradox: The complex software that landed Apollo 11 on the surface of the Moon in 1969 was not stored on silicon microchips, hard drives, or magnetic disks. Instead, every single line of code was physically woven by hand using needles and fine copper wire, essentially turning digital software into a piece of custom textile engineering.

During the height of the Space Race, MIT’s Instrumentation Laboratory faced a critical roadblock while building the Apollo Guidance Computer. Traditional computer memory of the 1960s was far too bulky, fragile, and volatile to survive the intense vibrations of a Saturn V rocket launch or the harsh radiation of deep space. A single cosmic ray striking a transistor could flip a binary bit, altering software commands and causing a catastrophic crash during lunar descent.

To solve this, NASA engineers developed a revolutionary hardware format known as Core Rope Memory. Software developers first wrote assembly code on standard paper punch cards, which were translated into a precise sequence of binary ones and zeroes. In Core Rope Memory, a binary 'one' was created by passing a fine copper wire directly through the center of a tiny, donut-shaped magnetic ferrite core. If the wire bypassed the outside of the magnetic ring, the computer interpreted it as a binary 'zero.' In effect, the software code was permanently hardwired into the machine’s physical geometry.

Because manufacturing required microscopic precision and extraordinary dexterity, NASA contracted Raytheon to build the memory modules. Raytheon hired skilled workers from the local Massachusetts textile industry, mostly women known for their expert embroidery and weaving abilities. Overseen by supervisors nicknamed 'rope mothers,' these seamstresses used hollow needles to manually thread thousands of copper strands through magnetic rings. The process was so unique that engineers informally dubbed the architecture 'LOL memory'—short for 'Little Old Lady memory.'

This hand-woven software proved virtually indestructible. Unlike modern digital memory, it required no electrical power to retain its data, and cosmic rays could not alter the code because a physical wire could not jump outside a magnetic core. With a total capacity of just 72 kilobytes of read-only memory, this hand-stitched computer successfully guided astronauts across 240,000 miles of space to the lunar surface and safely back home.
